common_name: Mercury Kentucky Bluegrass (Sports-Turf Cultivar with High Shear Strength and Shade Tolerance)

planting.note: Sow in late summer to early fall at 2-3 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in fertile, well-prepared soil; Mercury combines a high-shear-strength sod parent with a shade- and drought-tolerant Compact America-type parent.

directions: Mercury is a modern Kentucky bluegrass bred by crossing a sod-production parent selected for shear strength with a Compact America-type parent chosen for shade and drought performance, giving it a medium-dark green color, medium density, and unusually broad adaptability across sun and shade. It germinates and establishes faster than many older bluegrass cultivars thanks to large seed and above-average seedling vigor, and it forms a tough, tightly knit sod suited to sports fields and sod farms as well as home lawns. Disease resistance is strong against leaf and stem rust, stripe smut, and powdery mildew, reducing the need for fungicide inputs. Like other Kentucky bluegrasses it spreads by rhizomes to self-repair thin spots but goes dormant in extended summer heat and drought.

common_name: Quantum Leap Kentucky Bluegrass (Compact Midnight-Type Sod and Sports Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow in late summer to early fall at 2-3 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in fertile, well-prepared soil; Quantum Leap is a registered Midnight x Limousine cross combining both parents' dark color with faster lateral spread.

directions: Quantum Leap resulted from a cross between the dark, dense Midnight and the aggressively spreading Limousine, and it was bred to combine the best traits of both parents into one compact-type cultivar. It produces a very dark green, high-density sward with better rhizome vigor than Midnight alone, letting it fill in divots and thin spots more readily. That combination of color, density, and aggressive spread has made it a long-standing choice for sod production as well as golf fairways, sports fields, and home lawns across a range of maintenance levels. It goes summer-dormant under prolonged heat and drought stress like other Kentucky bluegrasses and performs best with regular fertility and irrigation.

common_name: Yellowstone Kentucky Bluegrass (Widely Adaptive Medium-Fine Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow in late summer to early fall at 2-3 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in fertile, well-prepared soil; Yellowstone was bred for performance across both low- and high-input maintenance regimes.

directions: Yellowstone is a medium dark green, medium-fine-textured Kentucky bluegrass selected for consistent performance whether it is grown under a lean, low-input lawn-care program or an intensively maintained sports field or golf fairway. It blends well visually and in growth habit with perennial ryegrass, tall fescue, and fine fescue, which makes it a common component of multi-species seed mixes rather than a straight monostand. It has been evaluated in National Turfgrass Evaluation Program traffic-stress trials, where it was assessed for canopy fullness and green cover recovery after wear. Like other Kentucky bluegrasses it spreads by rhizomes and needs a full-sun to lightly shaded site with periodic irrigation through summer to avoid extended dormancy.

common_name: Blue Note Kentucky Bluegrass (Compact America-Type Low-Input Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow in late summer to early fall at 2-3 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in fertile, well-prepared soil; Blue Note is a Compact America-type cultivar bred for good performance under reduced fertility and mowing height.

directions: Blue Note is a Compact America-type Kentucky bluegrass valued for its color, fine texture, and density under moderate rather than intensive fertility management, plus notably good shade tolerance for the species. It tolerates lower mowing heights than many older common-type bluegrasses without thinning out, and it holds a strong dark green color into winter thanks to good cold tolerance. Disease resistance to gray leaf spot and dollar spot is a particular strength, keeping stands healthier with fewer fungicide applications. It is used on sod farms, golf courses, and sports fields where reduced water, fertilizer, and pesticide inputs are a priority alongside turf quality.

common_name: Fiesta Cinco Perennial Ryegrass (Dark Green Disease-Resistant Turf-Type Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed at 6-8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in early fall or spring; Fiesta Cinco was bred through multiple cycles of regional selection trials for turf quality and winter color retention.

directions: Fiesta Cinco is a turf-type perennial ryegrass noted for very dark green color that holds up especially well through winter, when many ryegrass lawns fade. It was developed through repeated cycles of regional selection trials rather than a single breeding event, targeting a broad combination of traits including wear tolerance, density, and disease resistance rather than any single standout feature. It shows strong resistance to crown rust and pink snow mold along with very good resistance to gray leaf spot and red thread, diseases that commonly limit ryegrass performance in humid climates. Like other perennial ryegrasses it germinates quickly and is often used for fall overseeding of dormant bermudagrass as well as standalone cool-season lawns, though it fills in bare patches only by tillering rather than spreading laterally.

common_name: Wicked Cool Perennial Ryegrass (Fast-Establishing Fine-Textured Sports Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed at 6-8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in early fall or spring; Wicked Cool was a top performer in National Turfgrass Evaluation Program trials for fairway, overseeding, and traffic-tolerance use.

directions: Wicked Cool is a fine-leafed, very dark green turf-type perennial ryegrass bred for rapid establishment, forming a dense playable surface faster than many older ryegrass cultivars. That speed makes it a strong choice for fall overseeding of dormant warm-season athletic fields and golf fairways where downtime has to be minimized, as well as for quick lawn renovation. It carries improved resistance to gray leaf spot, dollar spot, and rust compared with older common ryegrass seed, helping it hold turf quality through summer disease pressure. As a bunch-type grass it does not spread by rhizomes or stolons, so worn or thin areas need periodic overseeding to stay dense.

common_name: Pennant II Perennial Ryegrass (Improved Successor to a Classic Turf-Type Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed at 6-8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in early fall or spring; Pennant II is an improved successor to the original Pennant, a cultivar noted in early NTEP trials for overseeding and heat tolerance in the transition zone and Southwest.

directions: Pennant II updates the original Pennant, a turf-type perennial ryegrass that performed well in early comparative trials for overseeding dormant bermudagrass in the Southwest and for heat tolerance in southern climates, with improved turf quality and disease resistance for modern lawn and sports-turf use. It keeps the parent cultivar's fine leaf texture and quick germination, making it useful both as a standalone cool-season lawn grass and as a fast-establishing overseed for warm-season turf during winter dormancy. It has been evaluated in National Turfgrass Evaluation Program trials alongside other turf-type ryegrasses for quality and wear performance. Because it is a bunchgrass, thin or worn spots need to be reseeded rather than relying on the stand to spread and fill in on its own.

common_name: SeaScape Seashore Paspalum (University of Georgia Drought- and Salinity-Tolerant Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Establish from sprigs or sod after last frost; SeaScape is a University of Georgia release that spent 16 years in development and testing before its 2023 commercial release.

directions: SeaScape is a University of Georgia seashore paspalum selection that finished as a top performer in National Turfgrass Evaluation Program trials run across multiple southern locations, as well as in earlier USDA-funded drought and salinity screening trials. It produces a dense, uniformly colored turf that holds quality across a wide range of mowing heights, letting a single cultivar cover fairways, tees, and roughs without the color mismatch that can occur when blending different paspalum selections. Like other seashore paspalum cultivars it tolerates irrigation with brackish or reclaimed water far better than bermudagrass or St. Augustine grass, making it useful on coastal courses and landscapes with salt-affected soils or water. Establish only from sprigs or sod, keep it consistently moist through rooting-in, and expect to manage thatch with periodic verticutting under vigorous growth.
sources: University of Georgia Institute of Plant Breeding, Genetics and Genomics

common_name: Aloha Seashore Paspalum (Wide-Bladed Golf Fairway and Lawn Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Establish from sprigs or sod after last frost; Aloha was selected in 1999 at the University of Hawaii's Lalamilo Research Farm and is licensed alongside SeaDwarf by Environmental Turf.

directions: Aloha is a seashore paspalum selection licensed by Environmental Turf alongside the finer-textured SeaDwarf, distinguished by a slightly wider leaf blade that still delivers a deep green, high-end appearance for golf course fairways, tees, and roughs as well as home and commercial lawns. It shares the species' strong tolerance of saline soils and brackish or effluent irrigation water, making it a practical choice where water quality would rule out bermudagrass or St. Augustine grass. It spreads by stolons to form a dense, self-repairing sod once established, and it tolerates close mowing better than most warm-season lawn grasses besides bermudagrass. Establish only from sprigs or sod in full sun, water frequently until rooted in, and expect to manage thatch buildup with periodic verticutting.

common_name: OKC1876 Bermudagrass (Drought-Tolerant Fall-Color-Retaining Hybrid Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Install as sod or sprigs from spring through midsummer, since OKC1876 is a sterile hybrid propagated only vegetatively; released by Oklahoma State University.

directions: OKC1876 is a hybrid bermudagrass released by Oklahoma State University, bred for improved drought resistance, wear tolerance, and fall color retention compared with older hybrid standards, with National Turfgrass Evaluation Program drought-stress ratings comparable to TifTuf. It establishes readily from sod or sprigs, forming a fine-textured, dark green, dense sward with good sod tensile strength for reliable commercial production, and it produces fewer seedheads than many older cultivars for a cleaner playing surface. It is adapted to golf courses, lawns, and other high-quality turf settings across the southern transition zone and Deep South. Being a sterile hybrid, it must be planted vegetatively and irrigated frequently until fully rooted in before tapering to a deep, infrequent watering schedule.

common_name: OKC3920 Bermudagrass (Freeze-Tolerant Ultradwarf Putting Green Cultivar)

planting.note: Install as sod or sprigs from spring through midsummer, since OKC3920 is a sterile hybrid propagated only vegetatively; released by Oklahoma State University for putting greens.

directions: OKC3920 is an ultradwarf hybrid bermudagrass released by Oklahoma State University specifically for golf putting greens, bred for best-in-class freeze tolerance among ultradwarf cultivars along with turf quality and ball-roll characteristics comparable to established greens-type bermudagrasses. It establishes with good vigor, fine texture, early spring green-up, and dark green color, and it can be mowed down to the very low heights putting surfaces require. Its improved cold hardiness extends the range where ultradwarf bermudagrass greens can be grown with confidence further north than older cultivars typically allow. As a sterile vegetative selection it must be planted from sod or sprigs and needs intensive management, including frequent light irrigation, topdressing, and grooming, typical of any ultradwarf putting green program.

common_name: Brazos Zoysia Grass (University of Florida Drought- and Salt-Tolerant Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Establish from sod or plugs (not seed) once soil is consistently warm; Brazos was discovered growing wild in the Florida Everglades in 2006 and released by the University of Florida after topping NTEP trials in 2013 and 2019.

directions: Brazos is a medium-fine-bladed Zoysia japonica selection that was found growing wild in the Florida Everglades and later developed by the University of Florida after it stood out among surrounding zoysia for its leaf texture. It combines drought resistance, early spring green-up, and extended fall color retention with disease resistance and tolerance of both shade and moderately saline soils, an unusual combination for a zoysia cultivar. It was a top-rated entry in National Turfgrass Evaluation Program trials in both 2013 and 2019, tested across multiple university programs in the transition zone and Deep South. Establish only from sod or plugs, since zoysia cultivars like Brazos are propagated vegetatively, and expect a slower initial fill-in than bermudagrass before it forms a dense, wear-tolerant lawn.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Turfgrass Breeding Program

common_name: Navigator II Creeping Red Fescue (Low-Input NTEP-Tested Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4-5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall in lean, well-drained soil; Navigator II is a strong creeping red fescue carried in regional fine fescue variety trials as an improved successor to the original Navigator.

directions: Navigator II is a strong creeping red fescue bred as an improved successor to the original Navigator cultivar, keeping the species' hallmark low fertility and water requirements while aiming for better disease resistance and turf quality in regional variety trials. Like other fine fescues it forms a fine-textured, slow-growing turf well suited to dry shade, poor soils, and low-mow naturalized areas where inputs are minimized, spreading slowly by short rhizomes to knit together a tighter sod than the strictly bunch-type hard and Chewings fescues. It tends to develop brown leaf tips if mowed too closely or too infrequently, so it performs best left at a taller mowing height or unmowed as an ornamental meadow grass. It is commonly blended with other fine fescues and sometimes Kentucky bluegrass in low-maintenance lawn and roadside seed mixes rather than seeded alone.
sources: Oregon State University - The Fine Fescues
